paras: The attempted lynching of George and Charles Pittman took place at Monticello, Lawrence County, Mississippi, in September 1903, when a mob twice sought to take the two Black brothers from the county jail. Officers removed the prisoners to Jackson for safekeeping, and no one was killed. Papers tied the mob's anger to the killing of J. L. Nelson near Brookhaven, of which Charles Pittman was suspected, though the Brookhaven Leader later reported that the witness said he was not the man.

The Pittman brothers lived on the farm of F. B. Smith in Lincoln County and, according to the Brookhaven Leader, ranged into neighboring Lawrence County, where they were "known as desperate characters." On Sunday, September 6, Sheriff Arthur Fox of Lawrence County and Rudolph Garrett went to arrest them near the county line on a warrant for disturbing the peace at a Black church. The brothers resisted, shots were exchanged, and one of them fled. The fugitive was later arrested by Smith and lodged with his brother in the Monticello jail.

About a month earlier, Jim Nelson, identified in a later dispatch as J. L. Nelson, had been killed "by a negro" three miles east of Brookhaven while in the company of Ord Pennington. The Leader also repeated a report that the brothers were related to Robert Charles, killed in New Orleans about two years earlier after shooting officers and citizens.

Sheriff Fox had Pennington view the jailed brothers. On September 16 the Leader reported that Pennington, "so it is stated," had positively identified Charles Pittman as Nelson's killer, and predicted he would be brought to Brookhaven "unless a mob makes short work of him in Lawrence." A Monticello dispatch to the Times-Democrat said instead that Pennington came to town on a Sunday but would not say whether Charles was the man. That night a mob demanded the jail keys from the sheriff, who put it off after identifying several of its members, and the crowd dispersed.

Talk then spread that Pennington had privately named Charles Pittman as the killer while refusing to say so to the officers. On the night of September 17 the lynching attempt was renewed, and the sheriff and his deputies hurried the two prisoners out of Monticello. They were taken to Jackson; a Jackson special credited the sheriff and two deputies, while the Leader dated the removal to Friday, September 18.

On September 23 the Leader reported, on information it called reliable, that Pennington now said Charles Pittman was not the man who killed Nelson. The paper admitted it had been told the opposite a week before and praised the sheriff for "bravely protecting his prisoners by the law's authority." No report of arrests of mob members, of a murder charge, or of a trial appears in the coverage.

The episode appears only in white papers of Mississippi and Louisiana, led by the Brookhaven Leader, which followed it in four items between September 9 and 23. The Leader called the brothers "notoriously desperate negroes" and in mid-September headlined its item "Jim Nelson's Murderer Captured." A week later it ran "Not the Right Man," withdrawing the identification without retracting its view of the brothers.

The Hattiesburg Daily Progress, under the headline "To Prevent Lynching," made no mention of the murder accusation and described the prisoners as "bad eggs generally" whose "latest escapade" had prompted a "lynching party." The Times-Democrat special, reprinted in the Leader, gave the fullest account and treated the murder allegation as the mob's motive. By October 3 a short paragraph in the New Iberia Enterprise in Louisiana described the brothers only as "negroes, charged with the murder of a white man," whom officers had hustled out of town "in time to save their necks."

The Leader's two local reports disagree on the arrest: on September 9 it said George fired and escaped while Charles was taken, and on September 16 the reverse. The Hattiesburg paper said the sheriff was wounded, but the Leader's first report said only that a ball went through his coat. The Hattiesburg and Times-Democrat reports call the sheriff "Garrett," while the Leader's local items name Sheriff Arthur Fox, with Rudolph Garrett as his deputy.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of George and Charles Pittman
bases: A mob twice sought the jail keys to lynch two Black prisoners, who were removed to Jackson before it could seize them (A4, A3, A6).

A mob acting without authority on a murder accusation tried twice to take the Pittmans from the Monticello jail, but officers removed them and no one was killed (A4, A3, A6); it was an attempted lynching.

accounts.label: Brookhaven Leader, local reports
accounts.gist: The brothers resisted a misdemeanor warrant and shot at Sheriff Fox; Charles was said to be identified as Nelson's killer and a mob was feared; a week later the identification was reported withdrawn and Sheriff Fox took both to Jackson.

accounts.label: Times-Democrat Monticello special
accounts.gist: A mob demanded the jail keys on a Sunday night and dispersed; after rumors that Pennington had named Charles, the attempt was renewed and officers hustled the prisoners out on the night of Sept. 17.

accounts.label: Jackson special to the Hattiesburg Daily Progress
accounts.gist: The sheriff, wounded when he arrested the two for unruliness at religious services, brought them to Jackson because a lynching party was forming.

accounts.label: Louisiana brief
accounts.gist: An attempt was made at Monticello to lynch the Pittmans, charged with murdering a white man; officers saved them.

framing.detail: The Leader headlined Charles 'Jim Nelson's Murderer Captured' and called the brothers 'notoriously desperate negroes' tied to Robert Charles, then ran 'Not the Right Man' and praised the sheriff for protecting his prisoners.
The Hattiesburg Daily Progress headlined 'To Prevent Lynching' but called the prisoners 'bad eggs generally' whose 'latest escapade' prompted the lynching party.
The Times-Democrat special and the New Iberia brief treat the murder charge as given and report the rescue as 'the negroes' necks were saved'.
